text: A SIEM correlation rule doesn't look at any one log line by itself — it looks for a specific combination or sequence of events, often across more than one log source, happening inside a defined time window. This lesson breaks down exactly what that means and why it needs all three of those pieces to work.

Take the classic example: 5 failed logon events for the same user account, followed by 1 successful logon, all within 10 minutes. No single event in that sequence is alarming on its own — failed logins happen constantly from typos, and so do successes. It's the pattern across time, repeated failures immediately followed by success for the same account, that looks like a brute-force guess that landed. Drop the time window and the pattern disappears: five failures spread across a year are just typos.

Lesson 7 covered signature-based detection, the kind Snort and Suricata use — a signature matches a single packet or payload pattern the instant it's seen. A correlation rule is a different tool for a different job: it reasons across multiple events and across time, often pulled from more than one log source, to recognize a pattern that no single event reveals on its own. A signature asks whether one thing looks malicious; a correlation rule asks whether a sequence of otherwise-normal-looking things adds up to something malicious, because real intrusions almost never announce themselves in a single log line.

Every correlation rule, regardless of vendor, is built from the same handful of pieces: the event source or sources it watches, the condition each event must match, the time window bounding how close together they must occur, the threshold or sequence that trips the rule, and the action it takes once it fires — an alert, a case, a notification.
Next, Lesson 14 takes those exact pieces and builds one real, worked correlation rule from scratch, in plain logical form rather than tied to any one vendor's query syntax.
